title: "Design Lab: A Maps and Route-Planning Service"
---

# Design Lab: A Maps and Route-Planning Service

Build a Go route API over a tiny synthetic road graph and a static tile catalogue. This is a maps-style service with separate map delivery, location lookup, and route computation. A road graph and a raster map image solve different problems.

## Define the first route contract

Accept `POST /routes` with source node, destination node, and travel mode. Return ordered edge IDs, distance in meters, expected seconds, and graph version. Begin with node IDs; coordinate snapping and geocoding are separate milestones.

Store directed edges with nonnegative travel-time weights and a mode mask. A one-way road has only the allowed edge. Keep immutable graph snapshots so one request never mixes versions. Reuse [Dijkstra's algorithm](../../08-data-structures-and-algorithms/10-shortest-paths-dijkstra.qmd) with a min-heap from `container/heap`.

A useful Go service boundary is:

```go
type RouteRequest struct {
	From, To uint64
	Mode     string
}

type Route struct {
	Edges        []uint64
	Seconds      float64
	GraphVersion string
}

type Router interface {
	Find(context.Context, RouteRequest) (Route, error)
}
```

Add a maximum expanded-node budget and check context cancellation inside the search loop. Distinguish unreachable routes from canceled or budget-exhausted computations. A `200` with an empty route is ambiguous unless source equals destination.

## Tiles, traffic, and cache boundaries

Serve immutable map tiles by `(map_version, zoom, x, y)` from object storage with cache headers. Validate coordinate ranges. Reuse tile bytes across requests instead of redrawing a map inside the route handler.

Apply traffic updates to a new weight snapshot and publish it atomically. Cache routes by graph version, traffic version, travel mode, and endpoints. A route cache ignoring these fields can suggest a closed road. Static speed-based weights permit basic Dijkstra; time-dependent costs need a separately specified model. A* requires an admissible heuristic, such as distance divided by a defensible maximum speed.

For coordinate input, snap to eligible road segments and include connector costs. “Nearest node” alone can choose the wrong side of a barrier. Keep address search and geocoding outside the initial implementation.

## Evidence

Use a graph with one-way streets, a disconnected island, a slower short path, and a longer fast path. Assert travel-time optimization chooses the correct route. Cancel a long search and verify prompt exit with bounded memory. Swap traffic versions while requests run and assert each response reports one coherent version.

Measure nodes expanded, heap size, latency, cache hit rate, and route changes under a closure. Scale by precomputed routing structures only after this baseline is correct; geographic partitioning must still support routes that cross partition boundaries.
